messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 26, Minh Tran came to treatment exhausted, divorced, and increasingly frightened by the life he had narrowed himself into since surviving a terrorist attack. He worked as a bank teller in a busy downtown branch, and the rhythm of the job suited the way he now lived: constant transactions, short exchanges, no silence if he could help it. He had begun volunteering for extra shifts, staying late to balance drawers, covering coworkers’ weekends, and taking on every tedious task he could find. He told himself he was being responsible, but he also knew what happened when he went home too early and the apartment became quiet. In the quiet, his mind drifted back to the day of the attack, and he would immediately try to push it away, changing the subject in his own head, turning on the television, scrolling his phone, doing anything not to think.

The attack had happened in a crowded public area while he was out with his then-wife on an ordinary afternoon. What stayed with him was not only the terror and confusion of the violence itself, but the moments when he reacted in ways he could not reconcile with the person he believed himself to be. In the chaos, he had made split-second decisions to get away from danger, and afterward he became fixed on what those actions said about him. He had come to believe he had failed some essential test of character. He did not describe himself as someone who had simply been terrified; he described himself as someone who had acted against his own values. That idea lodged hard. He had once thought of himself as steady, dependable, the kind of man who could be counted on in a crisis. Since the attack, he was certain that image had been exposed as false.

Over the following months, Minh became increasingly watchful in public. Walking from the employee parking lot to the bank entrance, he repeatedly glanced over his shoulder, scanning to see whether anyone was following him. If a customer lingered too long at the counter or if footsteps matched his pace on the sidewalk after work, his whole body tightened. He did not frame this as anxiety so much as necessity; from his point of view, failing to check would be careless. At night he rarely slept through. He would wake abruptly and move through the apartment checking locks and looking around to make sure he was safe. Even after convincing himself no one was there, he remained alert, listening for sounds in the hallway, unable to settle fully back into sleep.

His marriage deteriorated in the same period. Minh withdrew from emotional closeness with a determination that confused and hurt his wife. When she tried to ask what he was carrying, he shut down or said he was tired. Physical and emotional intimacy both became difficult. Being close to someone meant being known, and being known felt dangerous when he no longer trusted himself. He had come to believe that if he could act as he did during the attack, then he could not rely on his own character or judgment. He was ashamed of how quickly he became irritated, too. Minor frustrations at home could set off sharp, angry responses that seemed to come out before he had time to stop them. The divorce left him with a further sense that his life had split into a before and after, and that the version of himself that had once sustained a relationship was gone.

At work, the strain showed in flashes. Minh remained outwardly competent with customers, but coworkers noticed he was tense and easily provoked in the break room, snapping over small mistakes or abrupt noises. He compensated by working harder. The bank became the place where he could keep moving and not be alone with his thoughts. He took pride in being reliable there, yet even this had a brittle quality. He no longer felt capable in the way he once had; the confidence that had defined him was missing, replaced by the sense that he was only managing by staying busy enough not to feel.

By the time he sought help, Minh was trapped between exhaustion and vigilance. He was sleeping badly, spending little time with anyone outside work, and structuring his days around not thinking. What finally brought him in was the realization that the strategies he relied on were shrinking his life without giving him any real sense of safety. He was scared that this was permanent—that he had become an angry, mistrustful man who could not depend on himself and could not be close to anyone again. At the same time, he still held a quiet hope that if someone could help him face what happened without being swallowed by it, he might recover some version of the person he used to recognize as himself.
